text: The final plunge was basically a disposal maneuver to keep the spacecraft away from the moons, because a clean end mattered more than a dramatic exit. If Cassini stayed in orbit or drifted around, one chance hit on Enceladus could carry Earth-borne microbes or leftover bits onto a world where life might plausibly be, and that would be hard to explain away. Steering it into Saturn's atmosphere meant fragments would stay up in the gas. It had run low on fuel, so there wasn't an option to stay in orbit much longer. The point was to avoid a bad surprise.

Usually the stationary leg is where you take the load, and that’s what you’re feeling. The foot that is flat on the deck has to hold your weight, balance the board, and absorb tiny shocks from the street. The pushing leg alternates, but the standing leg keeps your body stable, so the lower leg and ankle muscles are working quietly under your feet. If your posture or the board angle makes the ankle rigid, the lower leg muscles may spasm or ache from being held in an uncomfortable position. Sometimes it is just your shoe pinching, or your foot sitting slightly wrong on the deck, and the body compensates with the other leg.

I’m not 100% sure which part hurts, but most skaters with this problem have tight calves or an overly stiff stance. The board tends to rock, and the stationary leg has to correct for it over and over. You may also be standing with weight too far back or too far forward, and that puts extra strain on the ankle and calf. If the hurt is sharp and happens in one spot, check the board wheels or a worn shoe, because a loose or damaged deck can make the foot jerk unexpectedly.

Most of the time it’s not a serious injury. Gentle ankle rolls and calf stretches help, and using a looser stance helps too. Keep the standing foot more centered on the deck, and don’t lock the knees completely. Letting the feet adapt naturally instead of forcing a perfect pose usually reduces the pain. If it’s the same every ride even without pressure, you’re probably just not comfortable yet, and the muscles are still learning what to do. I’ve seen this a few times, and it settles once the feet and ankles stop being so stiff.

Mostly, Afro-American isn't a claim that someone just crossed the ocean last month, or that their family kept an unbroken line of African names and traditions. It's an ancestral identity label, the same way we call people Italian American even if their grandparents left Italy generations ago. For Black Americans, the African part refers to the origin of many of their forebears in West and Central Africa, carried here through the slave trade. Some families can trace specific communities, but most can't, because records were sparse and communities were separated for a long time. That's what can make the term sound odd, like it's overstating direct cultural continuity. I'd say it points to shared heritage and historical experience, not a simple birthplace fact. People also argue over whether the label erases the distinct histories of Caribbean and other diasporic backgrounds, and whether Black American identity should include everyone who identifies as Black in the US. The shortened Afro-American form is just a clipped version of the same idea. It's about identity politics, not passport geography. Not everyone in the community accepts the term. Still, I think the label mainly names where ancestral roots came from, not where every family's great great grandparent was born.

Mostly from old army caches and border trade, with a few state arms dealers active in the south and northwest. Once the fighting spread, small arms leaked from arsenals or were traded between groups. They keep getting weapons because control of territory changes fast. Capture a depot or control a checkpoint and you can arm fighters. For many fighters it means defending villages and holding their positions, or fighting for their side. I'm not 100% sure how the flow changed in the last few months, but caches and border routes have kept the supply going.

People act like any drug that feels good must be rotten, but I don't think that's quite fair. Some drugs, like caffeine or a modest amount of alcohol, are pretty acceptable for many people. The uncomfortable part is the stuff with intense euphoria, and those are the ones people point to as examples. My take is that the high itself carries the downside, not some hidden poison.

It's also worth remembering that medicine and drugs aren't magically different. Most medicines are drugs. They only seem safe because the dose is tuned and the benefit outweighs the risk. If you use a normal medicine at the wrong dose, or use it every day without checking, the same warning signs show up. I mean, a painkiller can become the problem once the body starts needing more.

Reward circuitry gets pushed past its normal range. Opioids and stimulants do this more visibly. They make the brain treat the drug as a bigger reward than ordinary life. At first that's a good deal, but the brain tries to rebalance itself. Receptors adapt, you need more for the same effect, and baseline mood starts to sag. It's a bit like eating cake every day for months. At first it's nice, then you need more cake to feel the same thing. You get into a cycle where the drug works less each time, and withdrawal feels bad. The more pleasurable a drug is, the more the system has to adapt around it.

There's also the body side. Opioids can depress breathing, and stimulants push the heart and blood pressure. Alcohol wears on the liver. A drug that gives an enormous high is also moving major neural pathways, and that movement produces adaptation. The stronger the signal, the more the body compensates.

You ask why there can't be a drug with intense pleasure and zero adverse effects. I'm not 100% sure on this part, but I think the brain doesn't keep strong pleasure cleanly separate from its homeostatic controls. If it felt great the first few times and then the same dose stopped working, that's the adaptation talking. Researchers keep looking for safer options, but intense pleasure and no cost sit in tension. A drug with absolutely zero side effects would likely not be all that strong, or it would stop feeling so good over time. That's the catch, and I think most of the all drugs are bad talk misses that dose and frequency do as much work as the chemical.

Hi,

I get what you mean. The pain isn't a normal headache, because it's not just your head. Long shopping days overload the senses, and it's the deciding, walking, talking and crowd-navigating stuff, basically. That can turn into sore, tense muscles and a pressure feeling, especially if you stand for ages, carry bags, or haven't eaten. A hot, badly ventilated shop can make it worse. It's real, but it's more of a stress response than a classic headache. A quick snack and water might help. If it lingers more than a day or two, get it checked.

Best,

Honestly, the first part is a classic way to throw you off. Having just repeated and spelled out silk, you were still mentally caught up in the letter game, and then your brother asks something completely different. Your mind was still processing that task, so when the question landed, you didn’t carefully consider the correct answer first. The word milk was probably just the strongest cue for cows, and it slipped out instead of water.

It’s the sort of thing where saying silk over and over and spelling it creates a bit of a mental block. You weren’t being stupid or anything, just still on the previous task. I’d say it’s basically automatic association beating the conscious answer.

It could be less about the silk repetition and more that milk is the first thing that comes to mind for cows. But your brother’s setup made the mistake way more likely.

Thanks,

Hi,

you left it pretty open so I’m guessing this is a general “what should I know before buying a house” kind of thing, but send me specifics if it’s narrower.

Mostly it’s location, honestly, and I mean what the neighbourhood does on a Tuesday morning or after rain, not just a sunny Saturday. You can fall in love with a place and then find out the road gets flooded or it’s loud when the neighbours have guests. Don’t do that.

You should budget for more than the sticker price. Conveyancing, surveys, moving costs. A surveyor isn’t optional even if the place looks fine, because old houses can be hiding things, and a bad report isn’t the end of the world, it just gives you something to negotiate with or walk away.

Mortgage approval isn’t the same as cash. Get pre-approval and know the interest rate type. And if you’re going to ask for specific advice, tell me what you’re looking at and I’ll give you my two cents.

Anyway. Send pics or the address if you have one.

Hi,

I'm not a chemist, so treat this as a rough practical take rather than lab truth.

The big difference is dilution. The individual shampoo, conditioner, and bodywash each use surfactants and conditioning agents at strengths that work well for their one job. When a company builds that into one product, it has to split its active ingredients across washing, conditioning, and body application. For most people that means weaker lathers, less cleaning power, and less deposit of conditioning agents than when you're using each product separately. A 2-in-1 is already doing that kind of compromise, and adding a bodywash step makes the compromise even broader.

In practice, this often means the all-in-one product cleans okay but does not truly substitute for a good bodywash or conditioner, which is why I would not use it for my face or sensitive areas.

Also, there is no fixed standard for what counts as 3-in-1 or 2-in-1, so labels can be vague. If you want the most reliable choice, separate products are still the benchmark.

Cheers

Hi,
Honestly, they don't just watch it move, that would take forever. They use GPS on ground and stations on the continent, and they compare it every day.
It's like tracking a car's speed over time, and the thing moving here is the whole continent.
They do this with satellites, and the GPS receivers are super accurate. You can measure movement to within a few centimeters, which is how they catch the continent drifting a few centimeters a year.
In practice, they set up GPS stations in places like Iceland, which sits right where plates meet. The receivers log positions many times a day, and when you put years of that data together, the trend is obvious. That's a slow crawl, so you need lots of measurements spread over many years to be sure it's real drift, not just noise.
Also, scientists look at magnetic stripes on the seafloor, old seafloor spreading, fossil records, and the shapes of coasts.
But GPS and the older geological evidence are the main tools. We can even use this to show that the Atlantic is slowly opening up, and that North America and Europe are drifting apart. It also shows how geology affects the real world, and lets you see the world change.
Hope that clears it up.

Quick explainer on inbreeding and IQ, because the quick version gets it wrong. Related parents are more likely to pass the same rare genes to a child, so recessive variants can show up in double dose. It is like two copies of a harmful spelling mistake landing in the same child instead of sitting hidden on one side only. For many traits, a single copy is tolerated, while two copies can change brain development and neural connection patterns. This can affect thinking, learning speed, or attention. The link is population level, so it is an average association, not a guarantee for one family. Environment matters too, but inbreeding concentrates those hidden genetic loads. In practice, lower average scores show up with closer relatedness, and the effect grows as relatedness rises. For someone new, that much detail is enough. The science is many small variations stacking up, no single switch controls this.

The arm is not a pain-free spot, but injuries there are often easier to manage than injuries to the torso, neck, or leg. The arm is mostly muscle, tendon, and skin, and because it is a limb, you can rest it, bandage it, or move it slightly to find a less painful position. That practical control lowers the shock value. Nerve endings in the arm are dense, so cuts and bruises can still be sharp, but the pain is mostly localized. Injuries to the arm usually do not threaten vital organs the way chest or abdominal trauma can. In that context, adrenaline and the mind’s tendency to compare the injury with worse scenarios make arm pain seem smaller. It can still be very painful, and deep wounds to major nerves, arteries, or bones are a different story, but for many everyday injuries the arm’s controllability is the real reason it feels easier to bear.

Mostly it's the hemoglobin, honestly. Carbon monoxide grabs red blood cells' oxygen-carrying protein far more tightly than oxygen itself; that's the whole problem in one sentence. CO sticks to hemoglobin around 200 to 250 times stronger than O2, so even a low concentration in your breath can leave your blood struggling to carry enough oxygen to your tissues. Your organs then start feeling oxygen-starved while you're still breathing air that looks completely normal.

Carbon dioxide is different. It doesn't hang onto hemoglobin the same way. Instead, it moves through blood mostly dissolved and via the bicarbonate system, and your lungs and kidneys already have a steady routine for getting rid of it. So you can breathe in normal amounts of CO2 without turning it into the same kind of poisoning. High CO2 can still make you feel breathless, light-headed, or sleepy because your body tries to breathe harder to clear it, but it's not replacing the oxygen transport the same way CO does.

There's also a practical difference around work. CO is completely odorless and colorless, so you can inhale a dangerous dose without noticing. CO2 at least builds up in bad ventilation, and you often feel stuffiness or airlessness before it's an emergency. In small rooms or sealed spaces, both can rise, but the dangerous mechanism for CO is that it silently occupies the oxygen-transport seats.

I'm not 100% sure on this part about the ratio, but the point stands: CO has a much stronger claim on hemoglobin, and the body has no quick way to strip it off. CO2 is just something your system already knows how to clear. That's the main difference, and it's the reason one feels like a gas you can tolerate and the other can quietly shut down oxygen delivery.

When a plane hits the ground, the big injury risk comes from your body throwing itself forward and slamming into the seatback, cabin wall, or things in the floor. The brace is a way of stopping that lurch. You plant your feet on the floor, keep your knees down, and tuck your head low. Your arms go folded. The point is to make your body smaller and lower, so the aircraft structure and the seats take more of the crash energy, leaving your bones and organs out of the worst part. If you keep your head in and your centre of gravity low, you are less likely to hit your head or be thrown into objects. It won’t fix every injury, and I wouldn’t overstate it. But it’s a cheap way to lower the odds of a bad injury. Treat it as a reflex, not something you have to think through mid-crash. Follow the cabin crew’s callout and do it fast. It’s the kind of thing you practice once and then leave to your body, which makes it feel stupid until you’re in it. It is the same idea whether you're about to hit solid ground or water. In a water landing, the brace still keeps your body from floating forward, and you also keep your airways clear. A few seconds of doing this before the hit can matter a lot.

Mostly it's that "well known" comes with brand recognition, not just age. Pre-industrial trading houses were mostly local, family-run, and disappeared. Then industrialization gave us huge companies tied to railroads, steel, oil, appliances. That's basically where the recognizable names begin. I'm not saying nothing existed before, but those old firms weren't scaled to become today's household brands.

If you look at the oldest firms still active, a few pre-dating the industrial era survive, but they're the rare exceptions, not the rule. They mostly sold to nearby people, didn't have national branding, and often got absorbed. Anyway, that's the practical answer.

I still think the bank is the cheaper route, even when the dealership lists a lower APR. The rate is only the price of money; it is not the whole story. When I shopped for my last car, the dealer's number looked better than the bank offer, but the paperwork changed the comparison. They added a service package, gap insurance, accessories, doc fees and a prep fee. None of that is the stated interest rate, but it rides on top of the loan and gets spread across payments. On a $20,000 car with a 60-month loan, a few hundred dollars in add-ons can wipe out a one or two point rate advantage, and sometimes more. Sometimes the bank quote looks worse until you count what you actually paid in cash or added to the loan, and compare the full amortization schedule.

Dealers are trying to move metal, and the financing desk is a profit center. The lower headline rate can be a hook; the extra fees are where margin lives. With a bank you are more likely to get a plain loan with just principal and interest. You still need to watch your credit score, payment schedule and prepayment rules, but there is less to unbundle. If the bank quote has an origination fee, I would compare that against the dealer add-ons. That fee is usually one-time, while dealer extras keep bleeding money month after month.

I also think people anchor too hard on APR. A lower rate on a longer term can still cost you more in absolute dollars. I had a case where a 36-month dealer deal at 4.9% had a monthly payment that strained my budget. Switching to a bank and stretching to 48 months made the payment manageable, and total cost wasn't much higher. That is the trap. Get you into a payment you can almost live with, then let fees and add-ons quietly raise the total. A bank deal is easier to read line by line, and you can ask what changes if you refinance or pay early.

The bottom line for me is simple. Lower dealer APRs are often a marketing number, while the loaded loan includes extras banks usually skip. Unless I can get a clean bank rate or a dealer quote with no add-ons, the dealer path usually costs more. I have seen it too often to trust the sticker rate alone.

Look, I'm pretty much for it. The state-by-state patchwork is honestly the thing that bothers me most. You can have it in Denver and it's still illegal in some other states, and if you fly through that's a whole different conversation, or is it just driving? I've seen people argue they're getting caught. I think most adults should be able to grow and use it like you would keep a couple plants on a balcony, but the federal state split makes it feel like a weird game of musical chairs. I mean, why is the country still arguing about this in 2026, and not just pick one rule and be done? Half the time I feel like the debate is more about politics and old habits than about what the law is actually doing to people's day-to-day lives. Anyway, I don't know if a single national rule would automatically be better, but at least stop punishing someone for having a joint in a state where it's allowed.

My kids keep asking why muscles twitch, so I've been rereading my old nerve notes. Honestly, the body doesn't work like a car battery or a spark plug. It leans on tiny ion pumps that keep sodium high outside cells and potassium high inside. When a nerve fires, sodium rushes in, driving the voltage up, then potassium flows back out and the pump restores the baseline. Contraction is basically millions of these tiny ion swaps moving together. I'm not 100% sure I can make this land with a child, but that ion gradient is the part I actually get.

Mostly it's about finding a groove and hacking it up, honestly. People always think you have to dig through some dusty box of vintage vinyl, but for most electronic music today, it's basically a matter of pulling a file, cutting out a specific two or four bar loop, and looping it. I've watched a bunch of local producers do this at a studio. You load a song into a software program and drag the audio file onto a timeline. Then you use a slice tool to chop the sound into tiny little segments. You arrange those segments into a new pattern. The pitch and tempo get twisted to fit your new track. It's pretty much like taking a handful of Lego bricks from an old castle and building a completely new spaceship.

I think the legal side is where it gets genuinely tricky, and it's not just about having the beat. You need to clear the master recording from the label and the composition from the publishers. If you use a chunk of a hit song without paying for both, you're asking for trouble. I'm not 100% sure on all the fine print, but I've seen songs get pulled from streaming sites or forced to pay massive back money. 

The technical stuff is what I actually care about. You can flip the sample backwards, stretch it, or pitch it down. Sometimes you don't even change the rhythm, just the pitch. You can use special audio tools to stretch a vocal or a horn hit into something totally new. A lot of modern hip-hop and electronic music relies entirely on this kind of manipulation. You grab a famous snare hit, pitch it down, and that becomes the backbone of your track. It feels like a cheat code, taking a piece of someone else's magic and bending it to your own will. 

The whole process is surprisingly hands-on and a bit messy. You're just moving little pieces of sound back and forth, changing where the beats hit. It is its own art form, even if the legal red tape gets in the way. You can basically take a 60s funk break and make it sound like a 90s hip-hop beat by slowing it down and reversing the snare. You might also stretch out a vocal sample until it becomes a weird, echoing drone that sits underneath the new melody. That's the whole game, really. You take what exists and force it to fit your new idea.

I went to the doctor when I had a terrible head pain that wouldn’t go away. The doctor said the headache wasn’t really coming from the brain tissue itself, since the brain doesn’t have pain receptors in the way other organs do. So why did I feel such a strong pressure in my skull? The doctor said it came from blood vessels, nerves and muscle tissue around my head. When those get stretched, or when fluid pressure goes up, or when there’s inflammation, I felt that tight, throbbing pain. Honestly, I still get the occasional one from stress, bad sleep or not eating. And I’m kind of glad it’s just the surrounding tissue and not my actual brain.

I can't even tell you if the food is good, since we never actually got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, choosing this place specifically because we had a 10 p.m. show at the same hotel. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to pay at 8:23 p.m. We went back and just stood around until 8:40 before a staff member casually said we would probably not be seated until 9:15. It was just a party of two and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Honestly, absolute disaster. I mean, really zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which honestly felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was really disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but I feel like you can find those at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were actually interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Frankly, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles, and hitting it with the edge of the thumb makes it sound like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I’m typing fast and not looking.

I actually paid $38 for it and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard next to this.

Most of my job is email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while waiting. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version. I’ve sat through more shows than I can count before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed. The circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from any seat you get a decent view. Rare in Vegas. Some acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. Reminded me of Cirque du Soleil, just not exactly the “rip-off” way. If you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with more clarity. Clarity is exactly the problem though. What’s the story? I still don’t know. A dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It feels like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also way too much happens at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like stereotypical Vegas spectacle, more must be better, so they crammed everything in. Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay a second time. Apart from a few stunts it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago we called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my father. They never showed up because the woman who took the order wrote the address wrong. She meant 5407, but her handwritten 7 got read as 1, so the shirts went to 5401. The people there took the package to the local UPS store for return, then it was gone, and it was never seen or heard from again. We didn't find out until several weeks later. While that was being sorted out, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount wouldn't refund the original pair. The owner dealt with it then. He admitted the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were sent back. He said it was partly on us because we hadn't been friendly enough with the residents at 5401, four doors away. In the end, we disputed the first charge with our credit card company and eventually got a credit.
